notes:
I found good coverage of what verse-by-verse commentators say about every verse. On the two other questions, though, I found little.

- **Differences between traditions:** None of the sources I read describes a real Baptist, Methodist, Reformed or Lutheran position on this chapter. What I found are individual writers from those traditions who disagree on two questions: whether Jephthah was to blame for the war (vv. 3–4), and which Bethlehem Ibzan came from (v. 8). Treat these as one writer's opinion, not as what a whole tradition teaches.
- **Other views:** I didn't find any pages from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. The Catholic notes below come from Haydock and the Douay-Rheims translation, read on studylight and biblehub.

**Judges 12: verse-by-verse notes**

**v. 1**
- Ephraim felt slighted at having no central, honoured part in the win over Ammon. Guzik says they cared more about getting credit than about the job being done, and notes they had made the same complaint to Gideon (Judges 8:1–3). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-12/
- The Pulpit Commentary prefers to read "Zaphon" as a town name rather than "northward." It points out that "burn your house" is the same savage threat the Philistines later make against Samson's wife (Judges 14:15). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-12.html
- Gill says the Ephraimites were proud and restless, and especially jealous of Manasseh, the tribe of both Gideon and Jephthah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/12-1.htm
- Ellicott says the Hebrew means "were called." That is why the Latin Vulgate (the old Catholic Latin Bible) translates it "a sedition arose in Ephraim." https://biblehub.com/judges/12-1.htm
- Keith Krell notes that "us" is emphatic in the Hebrew. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_12_commentary

**v. 2**
- The earlier story never mentions Jephthah calling on Ephraim. The Pulpit Commentary suggests he asked when he first became leader, and they refused, partly because the fight looked hopeless and partly because they resented his leadership. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-12.html
- One commentator on this page adds that Ammon's raids hit Manasseh and the eastern tribes, not Ephraim, so "the Ephraimites held themselves selfishly aloof." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/12-2.htm
- Haydock (Catholic) notes on chapter 11 that Jephthah gathered troops from Gilead and Manasseh and also invited Ephraim. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/judges-11.html

**v. 3**
- Guzik: Jephthah's point is that God won the victory through him while Ephraim stood by, which shows how unjust their complaint was. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-12/
- Keil and Delitzsch explain "I risked my life" as literally "I put my life in my hand." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/12-2.htm
- **Writers disagree about Jephthah here:**
  - Defending him: Cyril Barber says Ephraim came intent on bloodshed and could not be calmed, and that fighting God's chosen leader amounted to fighting the Lord. Another sermon on the same page says the battle was the Lord's, so the glory belonged to God alone. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_12_commentary
  - Keil and Delitzsch say Ephraim had no grounds for its complaint and Jephthah had every right to resist with the sword. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/12-1.htm
  - Critical of him: Constable says Jephthah dealt with his fellow Israelites the way he had dealt with Ammon, taking revenge far beyond anything that might have been legitimate. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-12.html
  - The Life Application Study Bible says the war might have been avoided, and that taking revenge for an insult is just as wrong as the insult. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_12_commentary

**v. 4**
- The insult "fugitives" made Gileadites sound like outcasts or illegitimate. https://biblehub.com/study/judges/12-4.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says the King James wording here makes no sense. It reads verses 5–6 as a detailed expansion of verse 4: the Gileadites lay between Manasseh and Ephraim, so Ephraimites going home had to cross Gilead. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-12.html
- Fausset contrasts this with Gideon's gentle answer (Proverbs 15:1). https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_12_commentary

**v. 5**
- This is the third time in Judges that capturing the Jordan crossings decides the outcome (3:28; 7:24–25). https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60755/
- There is a reversal: the same Hebrew word that Ephraim used to mock the Gileadites as "fugitives" now describes the Ephraimites as they flee. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/12-5.htm
- Matthew Henry sees God's justice matching their sin. They crossed the Jordan in a rage and came back sneaking, never to see home again. They mocked Gilead's distance and were caught out by their own tribe's speech. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_012.cfm

**v. 6**
- **What the word means:**
  - "Shibboleth" means "ear of grain" or "flowing stream," and in English it came to mean an "acid test." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-12/
  - Poole adds that the word was natural to ask for at a river, so it raised no suspicion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/12-6.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary compares German dialects, where some say *stein* and others *shtein*. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-12.html
  - The Douay-Rheims, a Catholic translation, renders it "ear of corn." https://biblehub.com/judges/12-6.htm
- **The 42,000:**
  - Gill counts all who fell in the battle and the chase, not only at the river. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/12-6.htm
  - Arthur Cundall calls the number abnormally high for the period. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_12_commentary
  - The Pulpit Commentary suggests the war may have lasted a long time, but admits the number may be miscopied. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-12.html
  - Constable allows that it may mean "42 military units." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-12.html
- **Lessons drawn:**
  - Guzik: our speech should show we are Christians. He quotes F.B. Meyer that entry to God's kingdom does not depend on how we pronounce things. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-12/
  - Hawker (an Anglican): if Christ is in the heart, it will show in the lips, as Peter's accent gave him away. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pmc/judges-12.html
  - Several writers warn against church "shibboleths." Luke Wiseman criticises the Church of England for refusing Scottish ministers who were ordained without bishops. Another writer says Christians condemn each other over things as trivial as an "h." https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_12_commentary
  - The Pulpit Commentary pushes back: the test was simply a way to find out which tribe a man belonged to, not an example of making too much of small differences. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-12.html

**v. 7**
- The Pulpit Commentary suggests grief over his daughter may have shortened his life. It notes the ancient Greek, Latin and Syriac translations read "in his city Gilead." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-12.html
- One commentator says that despite the hard parts of his story, Jephthah is ranked by the apostles among the faithful (Hebrews 11:32). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/12-14.htm

**v. 8**
- **Which Bethlehem? Writers split:**
  - For Bethlehem in Zebulun: Keil and Delitzsch. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/12-8.htm
  - Kretzmann (Lutheran), who adds that Ibzan judged only the northern tribes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/judges-12.html
  - Guzik, quoting Cundall. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-12/
  - For Bethlehem in Judah: Matthew Henry, who connects the town's fruitfulness to the coming Messiah. Coffman also takes this view, following Josephus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/12-8.html
- **Is Ibzan Boaz (Ruth's husband)?**
  - Jewish tradition says yes (Talmud, Baba Bathra 91a). https://biblehub.com/topical/i/ibzan.htm
  - The Geneva Bible notes says some think so. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/judges-12.html
  - Ellicott says nothing supports it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/12-8.htm

**v. 9**
- Guzik: Ibzan made alliances through marriage, which shows his wealth and standing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-12/
- Coffman reads the sixty children as a sign Ibzan had several wives. He suggests Ibzan may have been building influence with other tribes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/12-8.html

**v. 10**
- Matthew Henry: the happiest life has the fewest remarkable events. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/12-8.htm
- Clarke counts these judgeships as about 31 years of peace, during which Israel grew corrupt and then fell to the Philistines. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/12-8.html

**vv. 11–12**
- Little is known about Elon, yet his tribe, how long he led, and his death are all carefully recorded. https://www.gotquestions.org/Tola-Jair-Ibzan-Elon-Abdon.html
- Guzik: God raised up leaders from different tribes, not just one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-12/

**v. 13**
- Barnes: being from Pirathon made Abdon an Ephraimite. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/12-14.htm

**v. 14**
- The old word "nephews" here means grandsons. Riding young donkeys marked wealthy, important men. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/12-14.htm
- Gill: Abdon lived to see his grandsons grown. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/erv/judges/12-14.html
- Barnes: these quiet years were prosperous and uneventful. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/12-14.htm

**v. 15**
- Matthew Henry: through Abdon, Ephraim begins to recover its good name, after producing no one notable since Joshua. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_012.cfm
- Guzik notes that Pirathon was the hometown of Benaiah, one of David's warriors. He links "the Amalekites" to the curse God placed on them (Exodus 17; Deuteronomy 25). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-12/
